summary: DNS over UDP keeps little server state but can cause truncation and retries, and enables reflection attacks. TCP avoids that, yet clients usually use it only for retries and servers close idle connections quickly. This standards-track RFC defines an EDNS0 option that lets servers and clients signal how long an idle TCP connection may stay open.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone call where the other side says how long it will hold the line while you are quiet, so you do not hang up and redial constantly.

questions: how long should dns tcp connections stay open
what does a timeout of 0 mean in edns tcp keepalive
how long can a dns tcp connection stay idle
subtitle: A DNS option that lets a server tell clients how long an idle TCP connection may stay open.

tldr.problem: DNS over TCP gives fewer fragmentation and reflection problems than UDP, but clients mostly use it only for retries and servers close idle connections after seconds. Each short TCP session pays a handshake cost.
tldr.mechanism: The edns-tcp-keepalive EDNS0 option lets a client say it would like to keep a TCP connection open, and lets the server answer with an idle timeout in units of 100 milliseconds.
tldr.outcome: Long-lived TCP connections can be used while servers still control their own resources, including asking clients to close by sending a timeout of 0.

today: RFC 7828 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2016, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be read with RFC 7766.

sections.title: Why Keep DNS TCP Connections Open
sections.content:
DNS messages can travel over UDP or TCP. UDP keeps little state on a busy server and finishes an exchange in one round trip, but it has risks. A single-datagram exchange can be exploited for a reflection attack on a third party. Response Rate Limiting lets some responses "slip" through with the TC (truncation) bit set, which makes legitimate clients retry over TCP. RFC 1035 set a 512-byte limit for UDP messages, and DNSSEC and other protocols make larger responses more common. EDNS0 allows larger messages, with more fragmentation.

TCP is less susceptible to fragmentation and reflection, but its setup costs an extra round trip: a single request and response goes from 1x RTT to 2x RTT. That overhead shrinks as more message pairs share one session. Clients that retry over TCP after truncation typically use the session for a single pair and go back to UDP.

This document proposes a signalling mechanism between clients and servers that encourages long-lived TCP connections while letting the server manage the state they require.
sections.plainLanguage: Starting a new phone call every time you have one question is slow. Keeping the line open for a few questions is quicker, if the other side agrees how long to wait.

sections.title: The Option Format
sections.content:
The edns-tcp-keepalive option signals willingness to keep an idle TCP session open for future DNS transactions, with the idle timeout set by the server. It makes no distinction between kinds of clients and servers. The idle timeout starts when the connection becomes idle as defined in RFC 7766 and is reset when that condition ends.

The option has three fields: OPTION-CODE (11), OPTION-LENGTH (0 if the timeout is omitted, 2 if present) and TIMEOUT, an idle timeout in units of 100 milliseconds in network byte order. Clients MUST use an OPTION-LENGTH of 0 and omit the TIMEOUT, so only servers send a timeout.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is a tiny note. A client's note just says 'I would like to stay'. A server's note says how many tenths of a second it will wait.

sections.title: Client and Server Behaviour
sections.content:
Clients MUST NOT send the option over UDP, and may include it in the first and later queries on a TCP connection. A client that gets a response over TCP with the option MAY keep the session open while idle, SHOULD honour the timeout (overriding any previous one), and should close the connection before the timeout expires. If the TIMEOUT is 0, the client SHOULD send no more queries and close once outstanding responses arrive. If the client sent the option and the response lacks it, the client SHOULD assume the server does not support keepalive and follow RFC 7766. Both sides MUST ignore the option when it arrives over UDP.

A server that gets a TCP query with an OPT record, with or without this option, MAY include the option in its response, and MUST give the timeout currently associated with the session. The value can change with local resources. A server SHOULD send a timeout of 0 when its resources are too low for more keepalive sessions or when it wants clients to close open connections.

Because RFC 6891 says a responder MUST NOT include an OPT record when the request had none, a server can only change a timeout when the client sends a query with an OPT record. A client that included the option in its first query SHOULD therefore include an EDNS0 OPT record periodically in later messages. Either side MAY close a TCP session at any time to manage resources.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks to stay. The server says how long it will wait, and can shorten that if it gets crowded, even saying 'please leave now' with a zero.

sections.title: Paths, Anycast and Intermediaries
sections.content:
Many network paths block messages with particular EDNS0 options, so a fallback strategy similar to that in RFC 6891, Section 6.2.2 SHOULD be used to avoid persistent interference.

For anycast servers, topology changes may disrupt long-lived TCP sessions more often than short ones. The RFC suggests that TCP multipath (RFC 6824) might let anycast servers anchor the server side to a unicast address.

DNS intermediaries that terminate TCP connections are RECOMMENDED to implement the option. An intermediary that does not, sitting between a client and server that both do, might close idle connections unnecessarily.
sections.plainLanguage: Some roads block unusual notes, so the client needs a plan B. And if a middleman does not understand the notes, he may hang up the call too early.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The option can be abused to ask for large numbers of long-lived sessions in a quick burst. When a server sees abusive behaviour, it SHOULD immediately close the TCP connection and free its resources. Servers could also monitor clients to build profiles of those that do not honour the timeout. Readers are pointed to the security considerations of RFC 7766.

A server can also use a TIMEOUT of 0 when resources run low or a denial-of-service attack is detected, which pushes TIME_WAIT state onto well-behaved clients. IANA assigned EDNS0 option code 11 to edns-tcp-keepalive, with status Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone keeps asking for far too many open lines, the server just hangs up on them.

fields.name: OPTION-CODE
fields.desc: The EDNS0 option code assigned to edns-tcp-keepalive.

fields.name: OPTION-LENGTH
fields.desc: 0 if the TIMEOUT is omitted, 2 if it is present.

fields.name: TIMEOUT
fields.desc: Idle timeout in units of 100 milliseconds. Only servers send it.
